TROUBLESHOOTINGITLE
In order to troubleshoot, a technician must have an adequate understanding of both the equipment under test and the test equipment being used. However, this alone does not make a good technician.
DISCUSSION

It is equally important for a technician to be methodical when troubleshooting. The technician must always keep sight of the overall troubleshooting task and yet, at the same time, be attentive to details.

Much time can be wasted if the technician jumps to conclusions without sufficient evidence. In most cases, you will be given equipment to troubleshoot with little information on the history of that particular piece of equipment.

Even if the user does supply a description of the fault symptoms, they may be vague or completely off base. You must acquire and analyze the symptons for yourself before probing into the microprocessor for the cause.

Occasionally, the fault may allow most of the microprocessor functions to work properly. The symptons may be specific enough to assure the experienced technician that the essential functions are working correctly while allowing the technician to deduce which area is causing the problem.

In this case, the technician may choose to begin investigating the suspect area without going through a more detailed check of the essential system functions. However, as a novice technician, you should be as thorough as possible in your observation of the essential functions.
A fault in an essential function may be minor enough not to affect the basic system operations, yet be responsible for a less noticeable fault.
Before you begin troubleshooting, think about the sections of the microprocessor and what role they play in the system operation and consider these questions:

1. Which components are not necessary for the successful execution of and interaction with the monitor program? Disconnecting all nonessential assemblies may make the machine operational again. If this was the case, you can deduce that the fault was in one of the disconnected devices of the interfacing signals.
2. How can you check and determine that the system is starting correctly when power is applied? Which components are essential in starting the system?
3. How can you test and determine that the keyboard and display are working properly?

Once you are sure you understand all of the sections of the equipment you are going to be working on, then, and only then, should you begin to troubleshoot the piece of equipment. ould you begin troubleshooting.
There are many troubleshooting techniques that you may use to locate faults in a microprocessor system. The technique presented here is a simple four step process.

Whether you use this method or another, the most important point is that you follow a logical sequence when troubleshooting. This four step technique will help you become an observant, methodical technician.

Compare the operation of a system to how it should operate. In other words, verify the symptoms. Do not rely on what someone else has told you is wrong. Duplicate the problem. This way, you can see for yourself what the equipment is or is not doing...-hand observations. Duplicate the problem. This way you can see with a trained eye what the equipment is doing or not doing.
The important point in this step is that you ARE NOT trying to fix the fault, only determining the symptoms. Once you have listed all the symptoms, go to Step 2.

Ensure that you have set up the system and test equipment correctly. Also, if you performed calculations in Step 1, verify the calculations are correct. be performed in Step 1, make sure that you did the calculations correctly. Look for any obvious mistakes.

To sum up, this step is used to verify that the symptoms observed in Step 1 are the result of real faults, and not caused by incorrect system operation or misuse of test equipment.

If the setup was not correct, make corrections and return to Step 1. Also, watch for software problems that might appear to be hardware faults. There could be nothing wrong with the hardware, just the software not properly instructing the hardware.

This is the step where you actually try to find the fault. Use the symptoms found in Step 1 to guide you to the area that could be causing the problem. Then use test equipment to measure and test the circuits. Once you think you have found the fault, go to Step 4.

After determining the possible fault, double check your work. Assuming you have found the correct fault, analyze the circuit with the suspected fault to determine if the fault could cause the symptoms you observed in Step 1.

If the fault would definitely cause the symptom(s), or part of the symptoms (you could have more than one fault), you can be assured that you have correctly identified the problem. Replace or repair the fault and repeat Step 1 to verify the equipment is 100% operational. bad components and repeat Step 1 to ensure the equipment is 100% operational.
If the fault could not cause the symptoms, go back to Step 1 to ensure that you observed the correct symptoms and then go to Step 3 for more measurements and tests.
Now that we have discussed the four step process of troubleshooting, let's discuss the proper handling of components found in a microprocessor system.

When troubleshooting a microprocessor system, it is important to understand the sensitivity of the devices that you are handling. Be extremely careful to avoid introducing additional faults that would further complicate your task.
There are certain environmental limitations which govern the proper use and storage of a microprocessor system. be stored and operated:
1. The system should not be stored in a dusty environment.
2. The system should only be operated within the manufacturer's specified temperature limitations.
3. The system should always be plugged into a grounded outlet.
4. The system must not be operated near an unshielded power supply of other equipment. Strong emissions from power supplies can force crystals to vibrate at the wrong frequency.
5. The system should always be turned off before connecting or disconnecting hardware to the system........................
Operating the system within the proper environmental limitations will help to prevent time consuming repairs in the future.

For example, a resistor may be hand carried, dropped, soldered onto a board using plenty of heat, and then have coffee spilled onto it, yet it still operates correctly in the circuit providing the coffee has dried!
However, you cannot handle CMOS ICs in the same way. Incorrect handling of CMOS ICs can destroy them by exposing them to electrostatic discharges from the body.

The following is a short summary of other component maintenance tips and precautions:

CAPACITORS: Ceramics, mica, and tantalum capacitors are not polarized, however, electrolytic capacitors are. If a capacitor is cracked, replace it. Be sure to observe polarity when installing electrolytic capacitors.
CRYSTALS: Crystal cases should be grounded. Crystals may be upset by strong emissions from the power supplies of other instruments and may vibrate at a different frequency because of this.
DIODES: Polarity must be observed when installing these devices.
FUSES: Don't rely only on a visual check; check fuses with an ohmmeter.........................................................................

HEADERS: Check that the header pins are straight before plugging a cable into them. These are the large rectangular connectors that are used to connect different sections of the 8086 microprocessor system together.
LEDs: LEDs are easily damaged by excessive soldering heat or by too much applied voltage or current.

RESISTORS: Value and tolerance can be determined from their color bands or markings. Replace cracked or discolored resistors. While they are very rugged components, exceeding their designed power limitation can destroy them. Resistors have a power rating in watts. Typical resistors used in Nida circuits are 1/4 watt...............................................................................................

SOCKETS: Check that ICs are properly seated in their sockets and not tilted. When soldering sockets in place, first ensure that the socket is positioned flat against the circuit board and then solder the diagonally opposed socket corner pins in place. Now the remaining pins can easily be soldered in place.

SWITCHES: Only clean with fluids approved for cleaning electronic devices. Do not use a pencil point to change rocker switch positions as contamination introduced between the switch contacts will impair its operation.

Even though, troubleshooting is part of a technician's job, the frequency of equipment failures can be dramatically reduced by eliminating potential problems before they begin. This is accomplished by a process called Preventive Maintenance.

As the name implies, this maintenance is accomplished before the system has a chance to fail. For example, suppose that your microprocessor is operating correctly and there are no signs of system failure.

However, you decide to measure the output voltages of the power supply. The measurements show that the power supply is outputting +8 volts to each chip instead of the normal +5 volts. Even though the system operates correctly, the output voltage may eventually damage some of the chips in the microprocessor system.
So, at a convenient time, you readjust the power supply. The action you performed was called preventive maintenance; you eliminated a problem which may have caused a system failure in the future.

Another preventive maintenance action is routine cleaning. Dust tends to stick to printed circuit boards. When a printed circuit board gets coated by a layer of dust, the dust becomes a thermal insulator and holds in the heat. This heat build-up can cause components to fail prematurely.
Dust, dirt, and other containments can also act as conductors which can cause arcing, shorts, and ultimately system failures.

In your studies of electronics, you have learned that multimeters and oscilloscopes are invaluable in determining correct circuit operation and for troubleshooting faulted circuits.
In each area of electronics, different types of test equipment provide the best means for circuit measurements. Digital electronics is no exception.

In DC circuits, the multimeter is the best choice for measuring circuit values of voltage, current and resistance. In AC circuits, the oscilloscope is invaluable for determining the characteristics of waveforms.
In digital electronics, the oscilloscope and multimeter are used, along with several other types of test instruments.

So far in this course, you may have already used a multimeter, oscilloscope, or a logic probe. While these are very useful troubleshooting tools, it is important to be aware of other equally useful tools and their capabilities.gic probe depending on the equipment that you used in the experiments. However, you should know what other types of test equipment are available to you.
The testing of digital circuitry differs from testing analog circuitry in several ways.
* Digital circuits use low DC voltages. 0, 1.3, 3, 5, and 12 VDC are the most common voltages encountered.
* Digital circuits normally do not have AC voltages present.
* Digital circuits normally do not require resistance checks due to the self- contained nature of ICs.
* Digital circuits often rely on timing; that is, the time relationship between two or more signals is critical for proper circuit operation.

* Digital circuits use ICs. Since ICs cannot be repaired, measuring input and output signals is the trouble shooting method used...........................................................................

Because of these differences, several special types of digital test instruments have been developed. Let's begin our discussion of digital circuit test equipment with a brief review of the multimeter, oscilloscope, and the logic probe.
The multimeter is the most commonly used test instrument in DC and AC circuits. However, it is not the most commonly used test instrument in digital circuits.
Multimeters measure DC and AC voltages, DC and AC current and resistances. Some even test transistors, diodes, and capacitors.

In digital electronics, multimeters are primarily used to measure operating power voltage (Vcc) and to check for open or shorted solder runs on printed circuit cards. Vcc is normally a DC voltage between 1 and 12 volts.

PC card solder runs are checked by measuring circuit continuity between different points on the card. Continuity indicates a complete circuit; no continuity indicates an open solder run or connection.......end in digital electronics is to use the lowest Vcc values that the chips can be made to run on. This helps reduce heat problems. Many circuits in development today are designed to run all the way down below 1 volt to represent a high condition.

The trend in digital electronics is to use the lowest Vcc values that the chips can be made to operate with. This help reduce heat problems. Many circuits in development today are designed to operate below 1 volt, which represents a HIGH condition.

Logic highs and lows may also be measured using a multimeter. A high is normally between 2 and 12 VDC, while a low is between 0 and 2 VDC. Remember, you must be aware of the IC family you are working with, CMOS or TTL for example.

Many ICs have a different range of values that represent a HIGH and LOW condition. As long as the logic levels are constant, a multimeter will give an accurate reading of a HIGH or LOW. will give an accurate reading of HIGH or LOW. G

But, if the levels are changing, or are pulsed inputs or outputs, the multimeter is of little use. Since there are more efficient ways to measure operating voltages and logic levels, the multimeter is normally reserved for checking circuit continuity and constant voltage levels, such as Vcc.
The oscilloscope is considerably more expensive than the multimeter, however, there are very few repair facilities that do not have at least one.

The oscilloscope displays a visual representation of an applied waveform and can be used to measure the characteristics of that waveform such as amplitude, period, and phase.

The oscilloscope is a very versatile test instrument, particularly well suited for troubleshooting digital circuits. The oscilloscope can detect abnormalities in waveforms that other instruments cannot.
Characteristics such as amplitude, rise and fall times, pulse width, period, and frequency can be quickly determined with the aid of an oscilloscope.
An oscilloscope can also be used to measure logic highs and lows as well as analyze the associated waveforms. In addition, pulse waveforms and square waves can be measured.

A big advantage of using an oscilloscope with a dual trace function is that two waveforms can be measured at the same time. Used in this way, the relationship of the two waveforms can be determined and analyzed.determined and analyzed. nalyzed. nd analyzed.

However, oscilloscopes have one disadvantage when used with microprocessor systems. Only one or two waveforms can usually be displayed at one time. This disadvantage is overcome by using an oscilloscope multiplexer.

Shown below is an oscilloscope which incorporates a 16 channel multiplexer. The multiplexer allows up to 16 signals to be viewed on the oscilloscope simultaneously. This is a great advantage when analyzing complex microprocessor functions such as the reading or writing of data.
DIGITALL

Also, signals viewed by the oscilloscope must be periodic. In other words, in order for the oscilloscope to properly display the waveform(s), they must repeat themselves in the same pattern over and over.

The logic probe is the least expensive of all digital test instruments. It was specifically designed for analyzing and troubleshooting digital circuits. It should be noted that logic probes only measure logic levels, not actual DC values.............................................................................................................................................................

The logic probe provides a simple means of determining the state of a logic signal: high, low, or pulsing. The probe is nothing more than one or more LEDs that illuminate for certain types of signal inputs.

A logic probe can indicate a high signal, a low signal, single pulse, multiple pulses or an open or bad level. Even though the logic probe is very useful for detecting faults quickly, it normally must be used with other types of digital test instruments to locate problems that are more than just a missing or incorrect input.

The logic pulser and current tracer are test instruments that inject and trace a pulsing current in a circuit under test. Their appearance is very similar to the logic probe, and they are often used in conjunction with the logic probe.
Logic Pulser/Current Tracerrrrrrrrrrrrrrrr

The logic pulser and current tracer are used to find points in a digital circuit that are stuck, that is, the point remains a logic 1 or 0 all the time. It is particularly difficult to isolate a bad IC when several are connected together. The logic pulser and current tracer make the job easier.

The logic pulser is used to inject a pulsating signal, (square wave), into the circuit if normal signal levels are constant. The current tracer is used to trace the current paths through the circuit.
An LED on the current tracer illuminates when the signal at a particular point is pulsing. No LED illumination indicates a fault and, by signal tracing, the bad component can be located.

The logic analyzer is basically a special type of multichannel oscilloscope used for displaying and analyzing complex logic signals and pulse trains. The analyzer can display these signals in several different formats.Logic analyzers, because of their expense, are generally only used to analyze complex digital circuits, where their expense can be justified.

The analyzer can display these signals in several different formats. Logic analyzers, because of their expense, are generally only used to analyze complex digital circuits, where their expense can be justified.

One type of format is the TIMING DIAGRAM. Several pulse waveforms are displayed in the correct time relationship. Dual channel oscilloscopes, can only display two waveforms. Logic analyzers can display many, depending on the make and model.

The second type of format is the BIT or BIT PATTERN. A sequence of 1s and 0s from a functional circuit can be compared to the pattern of a faulty circuit to detect errors. Oscilloscopes and logic probes cannot do this.
Another type of format that may be included on some logic analyzers is the CODED format. The coded format changes ones and zeros to either octal or hexadecimal code.

The code for a particular point in a circuit can then be compared to a given code in a technical manual or to code present in a functional circuit. Any difference between the measured code and the reference code indicates a fault.
The signature analyzer is somewhat like the logic analyzer without the waveform display. It uses the coded format by measuring pulse trains of highs and lows.

Signature analyzers are used to locate faults to the component level in microprocessor based systems.

The instrument converts a series of ones and zeros at a given test point to hexadecimal code. The code is called the signature for that particular test point. Then, by comparing the signature to the known signature, you can identify faults.
Again, the signature analyzer is only used in very complex circuits where the cost of the instrument can be justified.

The logic clip is a simple tool used to determine logic levels on an IC. The clip is attached to an IC where it makes contact with each pin. On the logic clip are LEDs or lamps, one for each pin connection of the IC.

The LED or lamp illuminates when a high is present and is off for a low. A pulse is identified by a dimly illuminated LED or lamp, depending on the frequency of the pulse. Logic clips are of limited value today because many digital circuits change states so rapidly, they appear to be constantly on when in fact they are turning on and off.ay are changing states so rapidly, the lights appear to be constantly ON, even though they are actually turning ON and OFF rapidly.
While test instruments provide vital information concerning the operation of the microprocessor and associated circuits, there are other tools technicians can use to make their jobs easier.

Visual inspections must be performed carefully before, during, and after troubleshooting. A thorough visual inspection can identify electrical, mechanical, or heat related problems as well as problems resulting from misuse.

Before you begin measuring circuit values with test instruments, look for damaged components. A burned resistor is a strong evidence of a power supply or transistor problem, or some other failed active component.

After troubleshooting and repair, do another visual inspection to ensure that the repair process did not cause any damage to the system, such as lifted solder runs, ICs or transistors not seated in their sockets properly, or drops of solder that might cause a short.

Diagnostic routines are programs used in the microprocessor to test the system. These programs are normally supplied by the system manufacturer. If not, and you know how to program a microprocessor, your own diagnostic routines can be written.
The only disadvantage of diagnostic programs is that the microprocessor system must operate well enough to load or execute a program. The advantage of diagnostic routines is time saving.
Most diagnostic programs will, at a minimum, identify what section is faulted. Some diagnostic routines even identify which components are faulted. No troubleshooting required!

Still, diagnostic routines should not be assumed to be 100% accurate. The technician should always verify the results of any software based diagnostics before replacing components. This is not necessary for board level replacement work...
